scenarios.title: Baseline deployment
steps: The referral completeness and appropriateness screening system is deployed across primary care centres in one health cluster.
Referring clinicians receive non-blocking prompts naming the fields missing from a draft referral before submission.
After six months, the proportion of referrals arriving with a provisional diagnosis, examination findings and investigation results has risen.
scenarios.question: Which instruments govern each node of this pipeline as deployed?
scenarios.expected_finding: Coverage is real but uneven. Obligations at SRC and C are binding and largely complete. Obligations at M and SINK are either scope-limited to medical devices or entirely absent, and PP carries the headline method gap. 17 of 35 concerns are governed by a binding, in-scope instrument; one further concern is governed by a duty for which no method of compliance is published.

scenarios.title: The re-identification that nobody can adjudicate
steps: A referral letter's free-text history reads: 'Patient is the brother of the mayor of [a town of 4,000 people] and was seen after the municipal council meeting.'
The de-identification stage removes the patient name, national ID, phone number, address, date of birth and medical record number. No direct identifier remains.
The sentence about the mayor's brother is not a direct identifier and is retained. The de-identified text is passed to the model, which runs in a cloud region.
A privacy officer asks whether this text was lawfully de-identified before it left the facility.
scenarios.question: Was this text lawfully anonymised, and by what test?
scenarios.expected_finding: Unanswerable on the current record. SDAIA's Guide requires removal of direct AND indirect identifiers 'in a way that permanently makes it impossible to identify the Data Subject'. IS0303 s11 requires a re-identification risk assessment before release - and that duty is binding and in scope, which is exactly the point: the obligation exists, and no instrument publishes an identifier schedule, a risk threshold, or a method by which it could be discharged. The operator cannot demonstrate compliance and the regulator cannot audit it. Under HIPAA Safe Harbor this sentence would survive the eighteen-identifier test too, which is why HHS pairs Safe Harbor with an 'actual knowledge' clause and an Expert Determination alternative. Saudi Arabia has neither. Gap G4, a method gap rather than an absence of law.

scenarios.title: Automating an existing inequity
steps: After eight months of operation, an audit compares appropriateness flag rates by originating facility type.
Referrals originating from small rural primary care centres are flagged as potentially inappropriate at roughly three times the rate of referrals from urban teaching hospitals.

Investigation shows the model was trained on historical referral acceptance decisions. Rural referrals were historically rejected more often - but predominantly for incomplete documentation, not for clinical inappropriateness.
The model has learned to treat documentation poverty as clinical inappropriateness. Rural patients now face an additional review step and further delay.
Published national data already shows a persistent regional acceptance gap: Eastern region 95.65% versus Central 85.43% in 2023-24, a gap that survived a system-wide sixteen-point improvement.
scenarios.question: What obligation required anyone to detect this before deployment, and what requires it to be fixed now?
scenarios.expected_finding: Nothing binding. SDAIA's AI Ethics Principles name Fairness, but are non-binding and sector-neutral. SFDA MDS-G-010 requires demographic alignment of reference datasets and multi-centre sourcing - but applies only to systems meeting the medical device definition, which a documentation screening tool does not. No Saudi instrument requires subgroup performance reporting for non-device health AI. The system would have amplified a documented national inequity with no regulatory tripwire anywhere in its path.

scenarios.title: The competitor who does not ask
steps: A commercial vendor offers a rival product to the same health cluster.
Their product automatically rejects any referral scoring below a completeness threshold, returning it to the referring clinician without human review.
The threshold was chosen by the vendor. It is not published and cites no clinical source.
A patient with an atypical presentation, poorly documented but clinically urgent, is auto-rejected twice before a clinician ever sees the referral.
scenarios.question: Is this lawful in Saudi Arabia today?
scenarios.expected_finding: Yes. Nothing prohibits it. Outside the medical-device route there is no Saudi obligation for human-in-the-loop, no obligation to make AI enforcement advisory rather than blocking, no obligation to justify an operational threshold against a published clinical source, and no obligation to disclose that AI made the decision. Our own system imposes all four constraints voluntarily. A competitor that imposes none is equally compliant. This is gap G2 stated at its sharpest: good practice in Saudi health AI is currently optional, and the market does not reward it.

scenarios.title: The referral that was complete by whose standard?
steps: A referring clinician disputes a completeness score, arguing the referral contained everything clinically necessary for the receiving specialty.
Both ask what the national standard for referral content actually is.
scenarios.question: Against what published standard is completeness measured?
scenarios.expected_finding: No published minimum referral dataset exists. MOH publishes referral urgency categories and response-time standards through Ehalati, but not content standards. CBAHI accreditation standards impose patient-transfer documentation requirements, but as criteria assessed by periodic survey rather than a specification a system can apply programmatically. Any completeness model must therefore derive its own criteria - the unsourced-threshold problem. Gap G11.
